speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of my riding of Nipissing feel victimized by the pricing practices of the large gas companies. In fact we might say that they are fuming.
I must confess that I find it difficult to account for price differences of over 10 cents a litre between urban and rural points in my riding and over 20 cents a litre between northern and southern Ontario. The people want to know: How could such large differences exist within a relatively small geographic domain and isn't it odd that the retail price of gas reacts very quickly to increases in production costs and very slowly to decreases?
What is even more perplexing is that there are no mechanisms in place to ensure that consumers are not ripped off for such a vital and necessary commodity. In fact, we are at the mercy of this virtual monopoly and what it can get away with in the marketplace.
The Minister of Finance said in his budget that he wanted to be tough on inflation. Indeed, he threatened the Public Service with job losses and back to work legislation. I wonder if the minister will be just as tough on his corporate friends when they give us unwarranted price increases, for this too causes inflation. Or, is it one set of standards for his friends and another for everyone else?

Mr. Speaker, the city of Winnipeg, the curling capital of the world,
is this week the site of the 1991 Canada Safeway World Curling Championships.
Ten teams in each of the men's and women's divisions are battling it out for a berth in Sunday's finals where world champions will be crowned.
Support from the fans has been extraordinary. A crowd of 11,349 last night at the Winnipeg arena raised the four-day attendance mark to 121,931, which eclipses the previous week-long record set at the 1978 world championships held in Winnipeg.
The combination of competitive curling, strong fan support, an army of dedicated volunteers, corporate sponsorship and excellent television coverage by TSN makes this week's curling in Winnipeg a truly unforgettable world-class event.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, this House accepted over half a million signatures for gun control.
Recently, too, an Angus Reid poll found that 80 per cent of Canadians and 88 per cent of women oppose easy access to arms in this country. The petitions and the poll raise the question of democracy: a concept in which the justice minister has been citing her belief throughout the Bill C-80 saga.
She fails to mention that her own Advisory Council on Firearms consists overwhelmingly of gun users. But, as the head of Canadians for Gun Control points out, "owning a gun does not make you any more of an expert on gun control than having a disease makes you a physician".
New Democrats say to the justice minister: physician, heal thyself, include the majority of Canadians in the advisory process: the Canadian Medical Association, the Canadian Bar Association, the Canadian Chiefs of Police, and not just a biased minority of gun users.

March 27, 1991
Canadians want democracy. Canadians want strong and effective gun control.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to the attention of all members and indeed all Canadians a national students' conference entitled "The Students' Commission". It will bring together four grade 10 and 11 students from all 295 federal ridings to one of our national workshops in Fredericton, Montreal, Toronto or Saskatoon during May and June of this year.
Thereafter, 96 representatives will travel to Ottawa to hammer out one final set of recommendations which will be presented to the Prime Minister on July 1.
The Students' Commission will be a viable forum through which our youth can express their ideas on a number of important issues facing our country today, such as national unity, the environment, the transition from school to work, drug abuse, the job market, as well as problems and promises of education, all as seen through the eyes of a cross-section of young people.
In particular, the commission offers our youth an opportunity to tell us, members of their federal government, what type of Canada they would like to see and what direction our country should take.
I know that all members will want the youth of their ridings to have every opportunity to know about The Students' Commission and to let it know of their interest and support.
* 3k *

Mr. Speaker, no problem can be more immediate yet at the same time have such lasting consequence as the inability of a growing number of people in our society to find enough food to eat.
While permanent solutions to this human suffering lie in the creation of a lasting world peace, investment in the individual, and environmentally sustainable development, we must find the time and the means to address
the fact that today and every day in Canada and around the world people are going hungry.
On Saturday, April 6, we in Ottawa South are organizing the second annual "Stop Hunger-Fast", a non-partisan hunger awareness event that features a 24-hour liquid only fast. Over this day we hope to collect food, pledges and volunteers for the Ottawa Food Bank and UNICEF. "Stop Hunger-Fast" will be held at the Herongate Mall in Ottawa, and we are hoping that our residents will take the time to learn about how we can stop hunger.
Hunger need not exist. Children need not be denied their future for a lack of food and senior citizens, for all their years of work and care, should not have to live in poverty today.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are facing the question of national unity. Now is the time for all good people to come forward and speak up for Canada.
One such patriot who has and continues to speak up for Canadians is Don Cherry. I am please to inform you, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Cherry is here in the House today witnessing our democracy in action.
The pride we take in hockey, our home game, is a reflection of the pride we have for Canada. Don Cherry has recognized this fact and is vocal about his feelings.
The upcoming Stanley Cup finals and the Canada Cup are fine examples of Canadian spirit. If Canadians could put as much effort into issues of national unity as they do their hockey, our country could stand together.
As Mr. Cherry says: "Unity is like a bunch of grapes; disunity is the pits".

Mr. Speaker, last week the federal government announced further measures for Canadian companies to participate in the reconstruction of Kuwait.
March 27, 1991

The key word here is companies. The Kuwaiti government will not issue individual working visas. Our government has indicated that it will not issue a list of Canadian companies awarded contracts.
I ask: How do Canadian workers access this wonderful employment opportunity that this government speaks of daily?
Canadian workers who have been laid off due to the made-in-Canada recession and plant closures are desperately seeking employment opportunities. Many of my constituents are willing to relocate to the Middle East, yet they are frustrated with the lack of co-operation and initiatives from the federal government.
This government is sending mixed signals to the Canadian people. This government is giving Canadian companies exclusive control over the contracts, and this government once again is ignoring the wants and needs of our own employable people.

Mr. Speaker, have you ever heard your constituents say that we can solve Canada's problems by decentralizing government? I have heard politicians and academics say that but not my constituents.
Some politicians say that we need to disentangle government, that we are over-governed, that we need to get the decision-making process closer to the people, and that that will eliminate waste and inefficiency. It all seems to make sense.
However, if we decentralize, what happens to our national social safety net? What happens to national standards? What happens to the equality of all Canadians? Should the city of Toronto's works department, for instance, really look after the Trans-Canada Highway? If it did, would that eliminate waste and inefficiency?
Personally I think we still need a strong national government.
5. O. 31 EXPO 92

Mr. Speaker, I rise again today to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to tell Canadians the truth about the boondoggle known as the Canadian pavilion at the World Exposition in Seville, Spain.
Yesterday I referred to a departmental document that said that the budget would rise by $10 million. Now it appears that the actual rise is even higher, from $33 million to at least $46.7 million, a $13.7 million overrun so far.
I have another document in my possession, also from external affairs, dated October 6,1989, which shows that the minister's officials knew the construction budget for the pavilion had been underestimated by 50 per cent. This clearly shows that the massive cost overruns plaguing this project are not just the result of unforeseen disasters in the past six months. It has been going on for a year and a half.
Yet at the same time that the government is spending more and more money on a pavilion in Spain which will be demolished at the end of the fair, the external affairs department has said that 306 positions will be cut in the next six months as a result of the federal budget.
I ask the minister responsible to confirm just how much the disposable pavilion will cost and how many jobs in external affairs will have been sacrificed to finance this apparently bottomless pit.

Mr. Speaker, today I have the pleasure to honour a colleague, a compatriot and a great Canadian. This man is a warm and kind friend to many and certainly a friend to all that is right and just in this country.
I am here to praise the man for whom the Canadore College Gerry Weiner Scholarship was named. This scholarship, which will be awarded in perpetuity, and for the first time in the fall of 1991, will serve to recognize the contribution and leadership of a student in the social service program in the area of human rights.

March 27, 1991
Oral Questions
I understand that the person responsible for scholarships and programs took this decision while listening to an inspiring speech of the Secretary of State in North Bay on the occasion of the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, March 21. It was not a prepared speech, but it came from the heart.

We are doing everything we can to promote national unity, and I know that people in my riding and other ridings in Canada will do so as well. Congratulations to our Secretary of State.

Mr. Speaker, the 7.6 per cent unemployment rate for the economic region of eastern Ontario is totally inaccurate.
Unemployment in Cornwall is over 15 per cent with 3,400 people looking for work. Many have lost their jobs due to plant closings and bankruptcies. The number of weeks needed to qualify for UI in Cornwall is 18, whereas only 10 weeks are required in regions where unemployment is at 15 per cent. In addition, only 21 weeks of UI benefits are provided to the jobless in Cornwall who do qualify for UI instead of the 37-week coverage allotted in a 15 per cent region.
When will this government stop using inaccurate data to mask the real picture of unemployment in Cornwall and other communities in eastern Ontario? When will this government improve the UI system which sets unemployment rates? When will it implement an economic development program to help the economy of eastern Ontario so that UI is not needed? The people want answers now.

subtopic: COMMENTS MADE BY RIGHT HON. PIERRE ELLIOTT TRUDEAU
COMMENTS MADE BY RIGHT HON. PIERRE ELLIOTT TRUDEAU
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a speech at the University of Toronto last Thursday, the former Prime Minister of Canada stated quite bluntly
that after the patriation process in 1981-82, sorcerer's apprentices persuaded Quebec it had been left out.
Now he accuses the Supreme Court, and the majority justices he himself appointed, of manipulating the evidence. This is not only contempt of court, it is an argument unworthy of a man who in the past was so quick to condemn injustice.
Furthermore, he justifies his Machiavellian policy by claiming he enjoyed the support not only of federal members from Quebec but of the majority of Quebecers as well. That is false. In March 1981, only 27 per cent of Quebecers supported patriation and 54 per cent were opposed. A year later, the figures had hardly changed: 26 per cent in favour and 55 per cent opposed.
If the former Prime Minister of Canada had tried to understand the aspirations of Quebecers instead of wanting to sabotage them, his policies would have had a better chance of surviving into the next century.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMMENTS MADE BY RIGHT HON. PIERRE ELLIOTT TRUDEAU
speechtext:
Before starting Question Period, I just want to share something with all hon. members.
Hon. members will know that we have customarily, for some time now, been coming in to open Parliament and to take prayers early. The reason for that is not to lose any time in either members' statements or in Question Period.
I am in your hands. I cannot proceed without a quorum, and I would hope that over the break you would all be determined to be here just a minute or two early when we come back so that we can get on with the business of the day.

That is certainly a good point, Mr. Speaker, given the fact that we all need some prayers at this crucial time in our country.
My question is for the Prime Minister.
March 27, 1991

[Translation\
There is one point on which there is a consensus in this House: it would be better to renew Canada than to have a referendum on sovereignty.
Yesterday, referring to his constitutional policy, the Prime Minister said outside the House that he had a very good idea of what he wanted to do and of the timeframe in which he wanted to do it.
Is the Prime Minister prepared to reveal to the House today what that timeframe is, since every hour wasted is an hour lost for Canada?

Mr. Speaker, as I said before, we appointed the Spicer Commission and the Special Joint Committee, the Beau-doin-Edwards committee, with very specific objectives. I said that at a given time we intended to put all this together with what transpired from the work being done by the Government of Ontario, the Government of Quebec, the Governments of Alberta and New Brunswick and so on, in a parliamentary process. This would give Canadian parliamentarians a chance to put forward national-not provincial-proposals that would reflect the needs of Western Canada, the Atlantic regions and the North, which might pave the way for a new Constitution or an amended Constitution. That is what we hope to do as we continue our work.
For the same reason, I urged the hon. member sometime ago to submit her own ideas on the subject- which would be a very interesting exercise-on behalf of her political party, and that is why all of us who believe in Canada are going to work together. We may work together as a team to initiate a process that will pave the way for a new but nevertheless strong and united Canada.
[English \

Mr. Speaker, in fact on this side of the House we want to play an all-party role. We want the Parliament of Canada to begin the real work of examining where we can go as a country.
Since last year, we have asked the Prime Minister for a larger role for the Parliament of Canada. His House leader has acknowledged that over the next few weeks it is likely the government will announce such a committee, possibly in the throne speech.
Oral Questions
Given that time is short, given that the constitutional clock is ticking, does the Prime Minister not think it would be better today to share his time frame and his ideas so that the Parliament of Canada can get on with the real job of saving the country?

Mr. Speaker, I do not doubt the sincerity of my hon. friend in regard to her commitment and desire to save the country.
One would have to be pretty far off base to fail to understand that this country, Canada, has been a magnificent illustration of co-operation between French and English speaking Canadians for 123 years. We are resolved to keep it together for another 123 years.
My hon. friend seeks a larger role for Parliament. There were two questions when we came back: one was a larger role for ordinary Canadians. The argument was that there has been too much involvement by many parliamentarians and premiers.
The Spicer commission was designed to invite comments from ordinary Canadians. It has been criticized by some, but I still believe that the Spicer commission will prove to have been an excellent initiative that will provide beneficial results and a major contribution to the debate. It is to report on July 1.
The second problem of substance we encountered not only with regard to the constitutional discussions last year, but with regard to the aboriginal discussions mandated under the previous Constitution was a flaw in the amending process. That is now being dealt with for the first time by a Senate-House of Commons committee.
It is doing very impressive work across the country. I saw some of their hearings from the territories and from Edmonton. Those two reports will have a very major and beneficial effect on the debate. It will be helpful to all parliamentarians.
Now that the Belanger-Campeau commission has reported, now that the Ontario legislature report has been tabled-I discussed it last night with Premier Rae-and other reports are in the process of coming in, the Parliament of Canada can be seized not only of these but of all initiatives coming from all parties and all citizens.

March 27, 1991
Oral Questions
I believe that we can put together the kinds of proposals that are responsive to the needs not only of Quebec, but of the west, the north, Atlantic Canada and Ontario. Then we can devise, perhaps, a new Canada; a better, more modern, more flexible and more united Canada.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Prime Minister said clearly outside the House: "We have a pretty good idea of where we want to go in the timeframes we would like to respect." Obviously, he has a plan in mind.
Does he not believe it is about time he shares that plan with the people of Canada? Does he not realize that if he waits until after Easter and until the throne speech, every hour lost is an hour lost for this country that we all love, Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the urgency inherent in the question of my hon. friend, but I indicated in the House of Commons in the past that this is a sovereign Parliament of a great and sovereign nation.
This Parliament shall establish the timeframes and not the legislature or political party in any province. We have a country. The country is called Canada. We are going to keep this country together by working together to the timeframes and the objectives of Canada.
In the process of doing that, we will by every reasonable means seek to observe and respect the wishes of others that emanate from other legislatures. That is not unreasonable.
The fundamental objectives must be set by legislators in the interests of all Canadians and within timeframes that all Canadians will find reasonable. I am not unaware of what is happening elsewhere, but I insist on the supremacy and the primacy of this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. With the Belanger-Campeau report, Quebec has lobbed the ball back into the federal court, all of which has taken place in a climate of political crisis and economic decline created by this government. Canada needs profound political change but it also needs economic change.
Unemployment and poverty are increasing in Canada. Fifty thousand children are going hungry in Montreal alone. My question is this: How does the Prime Minister intend to persuade Quebecers to accept his new political contract, considering that his economic contract and his obsolete policies have failed?
Mr. Speaker, that is the kind of comment all parliamentarians should try to avoid in this debate on national unity. Federalists in Canada and Quebec are not that numerous nowadays-
True!

-that we can afford to indulge in such mean-spirited accusations. We need all our allies. We need everyone. And I would urge the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard to contribute actively to this debate and do so positively and constructively. Instead of tarnishing the reputation of the federalist forces, help us build this new Canada!

Mr. Speaker, I can't believe this! The country is in a crisis, and all the Prime Minister has to offer is cliches.

The Prime Minister may not think the economy is important, but yesterday two of Canada's leading economists testified that this government's economic policies were: "destructive, caused vast damage, were nonsensical." The economists then went on to say that this government's policies would result in higher unemployment, more bankruptcies and a higher deficit. Mike McCracken and Doug Peters were the two economists.
The issue is, can a nation that is deprived of hope by its leaders, hope to hold together? The question is, why can this Prime Minister not bring himself to understand the inevitable link between national unity and a sound economy.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend asks if I understand the link between a sound economy and national unity. I assume that we all understand that. You do not have to be a Liberal or an NDP or a Conservative, I think everybody understands how important it is.

Oral Questions
My hon. friend says we have not demonstrated it. For example, today in the Toronto Star there is a headline which says "Economic optimism in Canada leaps to a three-year high," which means that the policies of this government are taking effect.
My hon. friend quotes a few economists in regard to the economic difficulties we are having. Well, we are having difficulties. We are emerging from a recession. Interest rates have dropped 408 basis points since their high, and we are now in the process of coming back.
Yesterday I had the privilege of spending an hour and a half with the Secretary-General of the OECD. He indicated that in its reports it would be commenting on the fact that the policies of deficit reduction, free trade and the GST of this government are contributing to a modernizing of the economy and that Canada's economy will soon be regarded again as one of the strongest in the industrialized world.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.

Yesterday, during Question Period, I asked the Prime Minister three times how he intended to obtain a mandate for restructuring this country. Today, it was reported in one of the newspapers that the Premier of New Brunswick and the Prime Minister had discussed the possibility of having a national referendum on the Constitution. Is that how the Prime Minister intends to obtain this mandate?

Mr. Speaker, I did not see the report but I have discussions on a regular basis with all provincial Premiers. Last night, I spoke to the Premier of Ontario who said that this afternoon he intended to make a major and, I assume, very useful speech on national unity. Of course, when we discuss these issues, we cover a range of possibilities, but we are not committed to one idea in particular at this time, especially since Beaudoin-Ed-wards is now considering the matter of the amending process, including referendums. The commission is to report in the near future, and with the hon. member, we will look at the results.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. Clearly Canadians need to know what is happening in all stages of constitutional development in his country. Canadians want to be involved and they want to know. One of the key issues is how we open up the constitutional process to all Canadians.
The Prime Minister has said that he will not work on a timetable other than Canada's timetable. But there is a timetable set through Quebec. Quebec has said that it wants the option of a referendum in 1992. We cannot ignore that timetable.
We also read today that there is a report from his deputy ministers who are working on the Constitution and have put in interim reports. Will the Prime Minister table those reports in the House today so that we can all share from that thinking and so that all of us can participate in that debate with full knowledge of what the Prime Minister is working on and what his officials are working on?

Mr. Speaker, I would have some difficulty tabling any reports from the deputy ministers inasmuch as I have never seen one. To the best of my knowledge there has never been any report submitted to me, to my office, or to the cabinet. I can assure my hon. friend that I have not seen hide nor hair of any report from any deputy minister with regard to the question she raises.
I will examine them when they come in and I will be happy to discuss them with the leader of the NDP in her capacity as a member of the Privy Council. We can decide the extent to which they could be tabled at that point in time.
I just want to point out to the leader of the NDP that contrary to her prefatory remarks, I never said that we were going to ignore Quebec's deadlines as set out. I said we were going to follow our own, and in the process of following our own, established by the sovereign Parliament of a sovereign nation, we will seek to accommodate the wishes expressed by others to the extent humanly possible. It seems to me that this is a fundamental Canadian question that ought to be decided by the Parliament of Canada.

March 27, 1991
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, of course it is a fundamental Canadian question and that is why this party has been pressing to make sure that all Canadians are involved: aboriginal Canadians, Quebecers, and the multicultural community.
But I say to the Prime Minister that the worst thing-and I know it is not the Prime Minister's wish or this government's wish even- for this country would be to see a Meech Lake II where the door is slammed on Canadians as other negotiations were going without the involvement or open knowledge so that everyone could participate in it.
His deputy ministers are working on reports. That is fine. There are other meetings going on. Apparently there are some talks about a referendum. We hear about one-to-one negotiations. Canadians do not want a sequel to Meech Lake, they want renewal. Will the Prime Minister be open with Canadians about all of the closed door initiatives as well as the open processes, the commission that we know is going on, and be honest with Canadians about the initiatives he is taking?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure that the hon. member meant would the Prime Minister be frank, but I think that we should watch our language in this veiy carefully.

Mr. Speaker, I will be happy to accept from my hon. friend any useful and constructive suggestions that she may have either in regard to procedure or in regard to substance. I have already indicated that-because the leader of the NDP has talked about the desire and the importance of listening to Canadians-we established the Spicer commission precisely so that it could listen to ordinary Canadians and it is in the process of doing that.
One of the matters that became very clear, beginning with the aboriginal processes in 1985 and 1986, and then in Meech Lake, was the flaw in the amending process. We have established a committee that is presently supported by members of her party in the process of looking for ways to correct the amending process.
Both of these reports, one listening to ordinary Canadians, another seeking to unblock the amending process, would be major contributions to putting forward the substance of constitutional reform.
The House leader and I have indicated that it is our intention at the earliest possible moment to create a committee that will involve all of the parliamentarians in putting this together on behalf of all Canadians. As soon as it is done, I will be inviting the member either to participate or to designate participation, but also to give us her ideas on how best this can be done.
There has been a lot of criticism of Meech Lake by my hon. friend. I would simply remind her that we are all great Monday morning quarterbacks, and her party supported Meech Lake all the way through.

My question is also for the Prime Minister.
He said yesterday that he gave no instructions to the Conservative member on the Belanger-Campeau commission as to how to vote on Monday on the question of a referendum in Quebec.
Many residents of this single great nation would like to know why the Conservative member on that commission was not told to vote against an early referendum. Will the Prime Minister tell us?
Mr. Speaker, I answered that completely yesterday in both English and French.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Prime Minister. Is the Government of Canada's position on the referendum a matter that interests all Canadians? Is the Government of Canada in favour of a referendum of Quebec's sovereignty, even in June 1992? Could he tell us something more substantial than he did yesterday?
Mr. Speaker, the question is so juvenile and hypothetical it doesn't deserve an answer.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Prime Minister. Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister said, as reported at page 19019 of Hansard:
March 27, 1991

-we are not abstaining from the great issues of the day. The government has taken a position in regard to the unity of Canada.
Canadians want to know why the Prime Minister says one thing on the floor of the House of Commons, while a representative of his government and his party does a completely different thing by abstaining before the Belanger-Campeau commission. Why the double standard, Mr. Prime Minister?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend from Toronto was here yesterday when I indicated that when the question on sovereignty for Quebec came up, Mr. Hogue, the member for Outremont voted solidly against it, along with other members of the commission, and it was defeated 17 to 15.
I also indicated to my friend something that he knows. He knows that Jean-Pierre Hogue is a very strong and very firmly committed French Canadian in favour of Canada's unity-so much so that it brings laughter from the Bloc Quebecois. They don't like strong French Canadian people who believe in Canada's unity as Mr. Hogue does.
Hear, hear.

They are going to find out, this little group over here on my right-and I am being charitable because Easter is coming-that this group is going to find out-

-there are a lot more French Canadians who believe in Canada than French Canadians who believe in destroying a great country like ours.

Mr. Speaker, all I can say is if he was a strong national federalist he should have stood the course right until the end and cast his ballot on behalf of the country that we all enjoy and the one we all love.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question is getting very close to imputing the motive of an hon. member. I am sure the hon. member would want to be careful.
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I return to the Prime Minister who also said yesterday, and I quote: "We have a Canadian agenda. We are not bound to anybody's agenda or anybody's time frame."
I ask the Prime Minister this. If he was so intent to pursue a truly Canadian agenda, why did the government representative abstain and thereby fail to stand up for a more realistic time frame that would give the Canadian agenda a better chance to succeed? Why condone a race against the clock?

Mr. Speaker, I thought my hon. friend, as a strong committed federalist, would take pleasure in the fact that a member, a colleague of accomplishment, such as Jean-Pierre Hogue, defended the interests of Canada, represented the Parliament of Canada with great dignity. Jean-Pierre Hogue is a very strong Quebecer and a very strong Canadian. He believes very strongly in the unity of Canada.
As the Speaker has implied, it is very dangerous for anyone to impugn the patriotism of a member of Parliament. I would remind my friend in any case, and I say this with some affection, to remember, as someone else said, that patriotism is the final refuge of a scoundrel.
Mr. Speaker, we learned in Le Soleil this morning that once again the Prime Minister and at least two of the premiers are secretly discussing a national referendum on the new amending formula.
Oh, oh.
Has the Prime Minister involved the leaders of Canada's aboriginal peoples in any high-level discussions regarding the Constitution and, knowing the dangers of excluding them, why not?

Mr. Speaker, I will tell Bob Rae of the indignation of the hon. member of the fact that he and I have been speaking. I will tell Bob the next time rather than call me to call you.

March 27, 1991
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, I am told that the matter was not raised with Bob Rae last night, but-
Oh, oh.

When Parliament returned last September the Prime Minister promised us one of his four pillars, that Canada would address the relationship between aboriginal peoples and governments. Yet his government has fobbed off responsibility for the off-reserve child welfare in the province of Manitoba, refuses to assert jurisdiction for on-reserve policing in Quebec and the Prime Minister himself has ducked every single question on aboriginal issues in this House over the last two weeks, including the last question.
Is this the kind of priority aboriginal people can expect from the Prime Minister and his government?

Mr. Speaker, the government is giving the very serious problems of aboriginals the highest priority and indeed the minister of Indian affairs registered another very significant accomplishment on behalf of aboriginals in British Columbia just the other day, and I want to congratulate him.
I suppose a question of equal importance is: How does the hon. member know what I said to Bob Rae? I think he has been spending too much time with Simon de Jong.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who says he has a good idea of his agenda for Canada. All Canadians are proud that our linguistic duality is one of the fundamental characteristics of Canada. I ask the Prime Minister, is it equally an important part of the Canadian agenda that our aboriginal people, our multicultural reality and our Charter of Rights and Freedoms be affirmed as fundamental to Canada's future?

Mr. Speaker, the three final proponents referred to by my hon. friend, I believe, are already in the Constitution and/or in the charter. Obviously that is already there.
With regard to the linguistic duality notion as being a fundamental characteristic of Canada, which it is, that very important precept was found for the first time in the Meech Lake Accord, which is one of the genuine regrets that I had, and I know many had, when it was rejected.

Mr. Speaker, unfortunately the other three were not found in the Meech Lake Accord where linguistic duality was located.

The Prime Minister knows Canadians feel left out of the constitutional process. They want to participate. They want to be consulted in an open process. Can the Prime Minister give us the assurance that residents in the North, members of cultural communities and members of native communities will be directly involved in the next round this time?
And women and children!

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend said "this time". I personally chaired two sessions with native leaders to obtain a constitutional amendment, and we were very close to success. If there had not been some last minute decisions in 1985 or 1986, we would have obtained this constitutional amendment that was so important to Canada's native peoples. So, do I believe it is important that the issue of economic and constitutional justice for native people is dealt with in a positive way? I believe it is not only important but vital. If we agree that this problem must be settled, we require the participation of all native peoples. And we intend to be very active and in urging them to participate.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. This week, the Commissioner of Official Languages reported that official bilingualism has been very successful, especially in federal institutions and the National Capital, but that improvements were necessary to preserve national unity. Does the Prime Minister agree with the commissioner? And if so, is he prepared to table the regulations for language of work and equitable participation arising from the Official Languages Act, regulations that are now two years late?
March 27, 1991

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I may remind the hon. member-I already explained this in the House, I believe yesterday or the day before-that we have tabled a major piece of legislation. This government has tabled an important bill concerning official languages. Mr. Speaker, in accordance with its mandate under Standing Order 108(2), the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs has the honour to present its fourth report. Having undertaken a study of arms transfers, the committee tables its report entitled "World Summit on the Instruments of War and Weapons of Mass Destruction".
This study was undertaken with some urgency, as the committee believes that we have the duty to do what we can to prevent the types of mass arms build-up that allowed Iraq to invade its neighbour and to cause tremendous suffering.
As a part of its post-hostility proposals unveiled in February, the government proposed a world summit designed to highlight the problems of weapons proliferation and to develop plans to control it. In the weeks since the end of the war, the committee has held hearings with a number of experts on the idea of a world summit.
I am pleased to say the committee supports the proposal and has made some suggestions which we think could strengthen its impact. We hope our suggestions will be useful in this regard, and we will work to ensure that Canadian policies are consistent with the goals of the summit.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the fourth report of the Standing Joint Committee for the Scrutiny of Regulations.

This report emphasizes the lack of legal authority for certain programs administered by the Department of National Health and Welfare and intended to authorize the possession of controlled and restricted narcotics and drugs.

The report notes that the department has been aware of the lack of authority for the regulations authorizing these programs for at least 15 years.
The report also notes that successive ministers have failed to seek parliamentary approval for legislation authorizing these regulations, despite the government's admission that the current regulations are illegal.

In their fourth report the committee categorically rejects the suggestion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the effect that departmental recourse to illegal regulations can be justified by his department's health protection mandate. The report points out that constitutional government principles make it mandatory for ministers and other public officials to enforce the law as it has been passed by Parliament, not as they would wish it to be drafted.

The fourth report calls for the revocation of the current regulations and their replacement by new regulations that conform to the Narcotics Control Act and the Food and Drugs Act.

He said: This bill concerns amendments to the Criminal Code. Specifically, it deals with the serious subject of the right of individuals who are in the latter stages of terminal illness to refuse or withdraw from medical treatment in order that the timing of a more natural death may preclude unnecessary pain and suffering.
In essence, this bill will address the question of whether we allow individuals in our society to have the right to die with dignity.

Terminally ill patients must have the right to determine their own length of treatment and physicians must, in turn, not be held liable for following the very wishes of their own patients.

speechtext:
Mr. Mr. Jean-Robert Gauthier (Ottawa-Vanier): Mr. Speaker, it is my duty to table today another four or so petitions on behalf of residents of my riding of Ottawa- Vanier who disapprove of Canada Post's decision to close down the branch located at 580 Rideau Street, which is part of my riding. These petitioners claim that this branch is serving not only a number of senior citizens homes, but also several embassies, three of which already strongly opposed the closure.

March 27, 1991

Mr. Speaker, I have tabled nearly a dozen petitions on behalf of constituents of Ottawa-Vanier asking Canada Post to reverse this unfortunate decision and I hope they will listen to good old common sense.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have three petitions to present today. The first requests that as the House of Commons has condemned the brutal and unacceptable Soviet crackdown on Lithuania and Latvia, Canada has suspended aid to the U.S.S.R. in light of Soviet military aggression in the Baltic States and the Canadian government does not recognize the de jure annexation of the Baltic States by the Soviet Union, and the Canadian government supports the peaceful restoration of freedoms in the Baltic States, and as the present Government of Latvia was elected on a pro-independence platform and enjoys the confidence of the people, the petitioners call upon Parliament to allocate and activate credits for feed grain to Latvia and the neighbouring Baltic States.
The next petition, Mr. Speaker, is similar in the preamble. However, in the whereases, the petitioners call upon Parliament to ascertain the specific requirements for medical aid to Latvia, allocate funds for the acquisition of required medical supplies for Latvia, and expedite the shipment of these supplies to the Government of Latvia.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition on behalf of several thousand residents of Labrador from a number of communities; Happy Valley, Goose Bay, Labrador City, Wabush, Nain, Makkovik, and other communities along the coast. The petitioners are calling on the Parliament of Canada to instruct the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to reverse its decision regarding the cancellation of Labrador services. They point out that the federal government, through the CBC, has seen fit to cancel all locally produced and locally broadcasted television material in the region of Labrador, and as Labrador is the only location in Canada's north to experience such a cut, and as there is no alternate source
Routine Proceedings
of local television broadcasts available in Labrador, neither a daily newspaper, nor a full-time local radio station, that these local CBC television services are essential and should be reinstated immediately.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, following the tabling of the Ways and Means Motion by the President of the Treasury Board, where we removed the tax on yoghurt but we certainly did not stop taxing books, which is to impose ignorance. Ikxing books is a terrible mortgage on our future, and I think we should do everything that we can to encourage reading-

Now that we have come to realize the extent of the problem of illiteracy in our country, now is the time to encourage reading, not to tax it.

It was with great regret that I will read once again into the record that petitioners, thousands now, call on this Parliament to remove the repressive tax on reading, which is a tax on intellectual property.
Mr. Speaker, please note that Canadians are not happy with the the Ways and Means Motion deposited today.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to present a petition signed by many of my constituents from Malpeque, Prince Edward Island. They are concerned about the post office in Albany and state that the Canada Post Corporation, which is presently reviewing the status of the Albany post office for conversion, its residents should not be deprived of adequate postal service due to the rural nature of Prince Edward Island.
These petitioners call upon Parliament to reject proposals which will decrease postal service to their local community, to take strong and immediate action to assure them that our post office, which serves a great need in their community will not be closed, put out on contract, relocated in another community, replaced with supermailboxes or any other inferior service.

March 27, 1991
Routine Proceedings IMMIGRATION

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the honour to present the names of close to 600 petitioners who signed this petition stating that thousands of east Europeans did enter Canada legally in good faith and did subsequently apply as self-exiles in good faith.
Self-exiles from Poland and other east European countries are unable to work or attend school while waiting for their applications to be processed, creating unnecessary hardship for both themselves and their sponsors. The processing time for many of these self-exile applicants is up to three years. The quotas imposed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration limit the number of applications being processed.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to request the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reciprocate on their good faith and speed up the process, remove quotas, and allow self-exile applicants to work or attend school while waiting for applications to be processed.
I am pleased that the minister responsible is present to hear these petitioners, and I hope that she will act on these before Easter.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a second petition. This is further to the thousands of Canadians who have already petitioned this House calling upon the government to issue a stamp in honour of Marie Sklodowska Curie who discovered radium. This honour can be made by issuing a commemorative stamp on the occasion of the 125th anniversary of her birth, which will take place on November 7, 1992.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand pursuant to Standing Order 36 to present to the House numerous petitions signed by citizens from North York, Thornhill, Willowdale, and several hundred from Guelph, Cambridge, and others outside of Toronto, all of them objecting strenuously to the unjust imposition of taxes on books, on reading, on literacy.
All of the petitioners humbly implore this Parliament to urge the government to withdraw the GST on textbooks and other materials that lead to literacy and culture.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a petition on the subject of the private member's bill introduced this day by the hon. member from Fraser Valley West. The petition points out the difficult questions confronting health care professionals, family members and terminally ill persons which have grown more complex with the advancement of medical technology. It calls upon Parliament to acknowledge openly the urgent need for changes to address the present denial of human dignity among thousands of elderly and dying Canadians by taking such actions as it deems appropriate to cause the government to examine the numerous proposals now being presented which would safeguard the right of every Canadian to control his or her own life to the end.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise again to present petitions signed by over 400 members of my constituency supporting the use of ethanol based gasolines. They want the government to make the oxygen content of gasoline at least 3.2 per cent and to ban methylcyclopentadienyl from further use in the automotive industry and as automotive fuel.
I am shocked that in response to earlier petitions the government has been responding using technology that is probably 10 or 12 years old and not up to current standards on the efficiencies that are involved in manufacturing this product or some of the end uses, one of which is a flour that can be used for human consumption, particularly suitable for Third World countries.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present petitions signed by approximately 900 or so Canadians, plus some visitors to our country. It is part of the "Put Canada Back on Track" campaign. The petitioners, who are from right across Canada, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to support the NDP plan to restore VIA Rail services cut on January 15, 1990, to maintain and where appropriate upgrade remote services on which many Canadians rely, to provide a legislative mandate for VIA Rail, and to make available to VIA the resources which it needs to become a modern passenger rail system in a class with those throughout the rest of the western world.
March 27, 1991

This is a new petition and perhaps the government can come up with a new answer.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a group of petitions from constituents in my riding from Melfort, Naicam, Mistatim, Hudson Bay, Spalding, Plea-santdale, Grandin, Fairy Glen and Lac-Vert, who note that the government is attempting to off-load some of the costs of maintaining RCMP policing in their area. They point out that the Government of Canada and Canada benefits by at least 30 per cent by the activities of the RCMP.
The petitioners request the Parliament of Canada to continue the sharing of this important national symbol and institution and that the federal government continue to carry 30 per cent of the cost of RCMP policing instead of the 25 per cent to which it is attempting to shift.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a petition to present with respect to the goods and services tax and its impact on Canadians, an impact which the petitioners are quite critical of.
The various ways and means motions which have been presented before the House today do not deal with most of these problems. They do provide some very important changes with respect to jigs, dyes and moulds, which are of extreme importance to my constituency and I am pleased to see, but they do not address things such as the need to provide an exemption for books, the need to see to it that this GST is replaced by a fair tax system applying in a fair way to Canadians across the country.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two sets of petitions which have been duly certified by the Clerk of Petitions.
In the first one, the petitioners point out that tax guides have been provided for a variety of groups with special needs. It also points out that students are a group with special needs with respect to income tax. They seek action by Parliament to request that Revenue Canada
Routine Proceedings
make available to students a guide that would be suitable to their needs.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to present the final 3,000 of
57,000	petitions which were submitted by the citizens of Windsor, the content of which you know, but I think it is important to re-emphasize the final paragraph. It says: "Wherefore the undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to take all necessary measures to preserve local CBC television broadcasting in Windsor and all other areas deprived of such service by federal government cutbacks and by the decisions of CBC management". I would remind you that we in Windsor have lost our sole source of local Canadian broadcasting and are, therefore, subject to dominance by American airwaves by the action of this government.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by people in a number of provinces: Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Manitoba and, as well, residents of England.
In their petition, the people humbly pray and call upon Parliament to support the New Democratic Party plan to restore VIA Rail services which were cut on January 15, 1990, and maintain and, more appropriately, to upgrade remote services on which many Canadians rely, and to provide a legislative mandate for VIA Rail and make available to VIA the resources which it needs to become a modern passenger rail system in a class with those throughout the rest of the western world.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege to be able to present a petition signed by several hundred people from places in Saskatchewan like Moose Jaw, Regina, Saskatoon, Prince Alberta and, in Manitoba from Brandon, Boissevain, Winnipeg and other points. These people have taken note of the spill of radioactive waste at Wollaston Lake in 1989. They found that the regulatory system that pertains to these kinds of events was grossly inadequate.

March 27, 1991
Routine Proceedings
Therefore, the petitioners are calling for a comprehensive, independent and public inquiry into uranium mining in Saskatchewan and in northern Canada in general.
As well, the petitioners feel that there needs to be an immediate EARP panel convened in order to look into the new mine at Eagle Point next to the Wollaston Lake mine.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I have the pleasure of presenting two petitions.
The first one states that since 1981, Canada's Dying with Dignity Association has been expanding and reflecting the concerns of Canadians for more widespread understanding of euthanasia.
It goes on to point out that many thousands of Canadians are kept in existence in conditions totally lacking in human dignity and with no resources for relief. The petitioners call upon Parliament to acknowledge openly the urgent need for changes to address the present denial of human dignity among thousands of elderly and dying Canadians.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the second petition I have is 45 pages long and contains several hundred names.
The petitioners are mainly old age pensioners living in mobile home parks who point out that the goods and services tax is being levied unfairly on their residences. They point out that the government is taxing shelter by virtue of the definition of mobile homes.
The petitioners also point out the government's failure to recognize the use to which mobile accommodation can be put and call upon the government to rescind the goods and services tax. They wish the prevention of taxing of shelter for persons residing in movable residences, including recreational vehicles, small trailers and houseboats.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise under Standing Order 36 to present yet another petition on VIA Rail.
The petition shows how widespread the support for VIA Rail is. The petitioners are from places like Winnipeg, Toronto, Kamloops, British Columbia, Fredericton, New Brunswick and various places in Manitoba, Thunder Bay and Calgary, Alberta.
These petitioners have not given up on VIA Rail. They have asked the government and Parliament to maintain VIA Rail as a present national network, to upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions.
The first one is from a number of residents from Saskatchewan who are concerned about the cuts made by this government regarding the Public Distribution Assistance Program which is threatening the future of weekly newspapers.
The petitioners are particularly concerned that weekly newspapers have been especially hard hit. In fact, weekly newspapers are, in many cases, the sole instrument for receiving news in a local area. They call upon this government to make some changes with respect to the mailing costs for these newspapers.

maintopic: FOURTH REPORT OF STANDING JOINT COMMITTEE FOR THE SCRUTINY OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition presented to me by a number of farmers from Saskatchewan who are very concerned that this government has removed oats from the Canadian Wheat Board.
The petitioners call upon this government to replace oats under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board and to give oats and barley the same protection under the Canadian Wheat Board that wheat presently has.
They further call upon this government not to remove oats or barley without this institution, Parliament, first having a debate and making a decision after a proper and open consultation with all the farmers in western Canada.
March 27, 1991

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

The member for Ottawa-Vanier and I had discussions earlier and I had his assurance. He is not in the House at the moment but there may be another member of the party who can speak on his behalf. speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will keep my remarks very short. This piece of legislation we are dealing with, Bill C-98, has had considerable study throughout the country going back to January 9, 1990 when the committee was formed. We have had a lot of consultation right across the country with provincial governments, producers, and the federal government.
I would like to read into the record, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, the names of those people who contributed so much time and help to the process we have just come through: from the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Don Downe; from the National Farmers Union, Gil Pedersen; from the Atlantic Grains Council, George Burris, secretary-manager of the council; from Quebec, Claude Lafleur; from Ontario, Terry Daynard, executive vice-president of the Ontario Corn Producers' Association; Roger George of the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, an organization which represents many farmers and producers across this country; and Larry Miehls from the Ontario Soybean Growers' Marketing Board.
From the prairies we had Gordon Cresswell and Bill Duke who served with the Western Canadian Wheat Growers' Association; Ken Edie from the Manitoba Pool Elevators; Alex Graham from the Alberta Wheat Pool and Terry Hanson from the Advisory Committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. Also we had Ed Armstrong, Western Barley Growers' Association; Bob Hopely of the Western Grain Stabilization Advisory Committee and Keith Lewis, the past president of the Prairie Canola Board; Owen McAulay from Keystone Agriculture Products; Roy Piper from the United Grain Growers; Barry Seneft, director of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool; Frank Spanbauer from Western Canada Pulse Growers and Brian Haddow from the B.C. Federation of Agriculture.

March 27, 1991
Government Orders
You forgot us. We helped.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Yes. Mr. Speaker, I want to say, as well, that we thank all parties in the House of Commons for the co-operation they extended to us. They recognize the importance of this legislation and how necessary it is to have it implemented as quickly as possible.
Many things have been said about the legislation. We have been accused of hurrying it through the House of Commons in the process. As I said before, from the timeframe and the consultations held with producers across this country, the 19 producers on that committee, I believe this is legislation that everybody should be very proud of because they played a very major role in its development.
It is now up to us to give quick passage to Bill C-98, and allow the Senate to deliberate on the bill. It is the first time in a long while the farmers and producers of this country have had such a major, comprehensive piece of legislation that offers the long-term security and bankable programs this legislation does.
We wish more provinces would offer the NISA program, because we believe that GRIP and NISA are compatible with one another and would give that much more security to the farm economy as well.
I will close my remarks by asking my colleagues if they could give quick passage to this legislation, because I believe it is absolutely necessary and the producers are looking for it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words at the third reading stage of Bill C-98, the Farm Income Protection Act. This is extremely important legislation.
Unfortunately it is not legislation which spells out exactly what arrangements will be provided to producers of agriculture products, but rather provides a framework for the government to put in place agreements with provincial governments and with producers groups. From that point of view, I think it really circumvents Parliament and does not allow for the normal kinds of inputs to be made for producers in stabilizing their incomes.
The proposals planned under this bill, the Gross Revenue Insurance Program and the Net Income Stabilization Account and the third line of defence, or the
special arrangements provisions probably will be made to work.
I am exceedingly skeptical as to whether the agreements that have been put in place will be in place three or four years from now. I think there will have to be massive modifications to them.
I believe there is a great deal of concern among producers as to just how serious the government is about this legislation. There are those who think there will be a massive payout in 1992 and 1993. Those are election years. After that there will be very little pay-out because of the structure and the arrangements. Whether the GRIP and NISA programs survive no one knows at this time.
There is one overriding consideration and it is that the situation for Canadian grains and oilseed producers is so desperate that whatever the proposal being offered by this government and by the provincial governments involved, producers need it desperately at this time.
The net farm income this year is projected to drop by 54 per cent from about $4 billion to $2 billion. This is an industry that at the retail level has something like $45 billion. At the farm gate level there is some $22 billion. Out of that $22 billion only $2 billion is there as total net farm income. The Department of Agriculture has projected no net farm income for provinces like Saskatchewan and Manitoba this year.
The situation is exceedingly desperate. Farmers are being forced to take GRIP this year because the initial price for grain is not going to be revealed until late July. The world farm gate price for wheat may be as low as $90 or $95 a tonne, lower than it has been in real terms since the 1930s. The situation is so desperate that producers feel they have absolutely no choice.
If we look at the three levels of support, GRIP and NISA are designed to stabilize farm incomes and level out the low years with the high years of income. The government has lost all credibility with the special arrangements committee, special arrangements or deficiency payments that are being proposed because it has not made an announcement. It is now the end of March. It is questionable whether any assistance will be made available in time for the seeding next month or early May.
March 27, 1991

That destroys the credibility of the whole three-stage level of support, especially with net farm income dropping by over 50 per cent this year. Many farmers feel they have to take the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, even though the premiums are very high, because of the tremendous uncertainty and the question in their minds is: "Is the government really going to provide any additional assistance?"
Today the minister had a backbencher put a question concerning western grain stabilization fund. He announced that there was going to be $158 million distributed under the western grain stabilization fund this spring. That would be an interim payment in this particular crop year. It sounds like a lot of money. When we realize that net farm income is dropping by $2 billion, and the minister's own advisory committee on interim financial support is recommending at least $1 billion or $1.2 billion, it is not very much. Unless the minister comes through with a major payment, the situation this spring for literally tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of producers is going to be very bleak.
On this side of the House we are concerned about executive federalism, where the government gets legislation like this which puts it in the position to make all kinds of deals without hardly a nod to Parliament. Fortunately, the government has accepted a couple of amendments from this side of the House. One is by the member for Prince Edward-Hastings recommending that there be an ongoing review of the legislation. The one that provided specifically for a review and report to Parliament by 1993 was not accepted, but we hope the amendment that was put by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings will have the effect of providing that kind of interim review.
I do not think there is very much confidence among producers as to what is going to happen with this legislation. I am told that in the central part of Alberta many producers will not take the program. I met with a number of producers in western Canada over the weekend and the split was interesting. Some were going to take the program because they were in such a desperate situation. Others who were in a stronger position financially said they saw the benefit this year, but thought they would be paying for four years and, at the end of the day,
Government Orders
they would not profit much by enrolling in the program. So there is great skepticism and great uncertainty.
The one amendment, which was put by our side of the House and accepted, provides for the government to be required, with the concurrence of the provinces, to table each agreement. At least we have the agreements with whatever number of provinces take it on.
There is great concern that the legislation will not be national in scope. There is provision for it. We have some five or six provinces who have, so far, indicated they will take the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, but only one has agreed to take the Net Income Stabilization Program, that being Saskatchewan. Whether the program will ever be national in scope the way that the western grain stabilization and the Agriculture Stabilization Act worked in tandem, only time will tell. That is part of the uncertainty with the whole arrangement.
The bill sets out laudable objectives: it should be market neutral; it should be production neutral; it should respect our international trade arrangements; it should be environmentally sustainable. Yet some groups who came before the committee were able to put very convincing arguments that none of these objectives will be met, at least in the initial year. That is why the need for a very capable and competent review.
Already there are important and credible agriculture forecasting groups saying that the bill is going to encourage greater production of wheat and it is going to ignore market signals. It would be most unfortunate if that were to occur this year when wheat is at $2.50 a bushel rather than $4 or $5 a bushel and that should not trigger a signal for an increased production of two million acres of wheat rather than a reduction of one million acres of wheat as probably would have happened without the GRIP program being in place.
There are a number of other amendments which the government did not accept. One is to protect the integrity of individual producer's income tax confidentiality. This bill will provide that the ordinary crop insurance authorities in each province will simply be able to trigger an individual producer's income tax files. I am not sure that is necessary or desirable. I am sure it is not desirable and I doubt that it is even necessary.

March 27, 1991
Government Orders
We had proposed as well that the government should not be allowing NISA, which is a funded program where the government matches dollar for dollar certain amounts of funding, to be made available to other than Canadian citizens or permanent residents of Canada. The government did not accept those amendments.
We look at the bill believing that it is a framework legislation that can provide for agreements. We are not certain how effective the legislation will be and whether the objectives will be met. On the other hand, we believe that the government has an immediate responsibility to provide cash assistance before the crop season begins this spring. Because of its urgency, we hope that the government will act and bring this legislation back to the House from time to time to be amended, as needed, or at least to have the agreements amended so that we will be able to make the necessary adjustments. With the wide variety of growing situations and market circumstances and other aspects involved in this, and at a time of incredible cash flow shortage, there is not much confidence or belief that this legislation will stand as it is for very long without amendments to those agreements.
We want to see the legislation pass so that the benefits can be made available to producers. We think it will require adjustments and changes not very far down the road, but we are pleased to see it pass at third reading today and get on the road to providing assistance either later this fall or certainly in the next crop year to remedy in that crop year what has been lost in this particular crop year. During the past two years the government has chopped back in a crude and violent way government support programs by some $1.6 billion. That is why there is an emergency today for Canadian grain and oilseed producers.
This legislation is not going to correct that immediate problem. We require assistance immediately, before the planting season this spring. If this legislation works the way the government believes it will, hopefully it will be useful in the next crop year 1991-92.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I attended a press conference where I and a number of my colleagues from this House who had made a recent trip to Sudan and Ethiopia were putting
before our country the needs of those particular countries for food. It is recognized that if we do not get a couple of million tonnes of food to those countries in the next few months, as many as a million people will die.
There are 12 million people in those two countries that are being affected by famine, a famine that is considered to be even worse than the one in 1984-85 in which one million people died. This is thought to be a worse situation because of unco-operative governments and the wars that are going on in those areas. We in the prairies and in Canada grow over 50 million tonnes of grain, of which we export up to 30 million tonnes. Our contribution to world food is fairly small compared to the amount that we actually grow.
What we are talking about today is a system which will allow the farmers in Canada to survive. It is almost ridiculous that we find ourselves working on a plan that is supposed to help in the survival of the food producers in our country when there is such a great need in the world for the food that we produce.
Obviously there is something wrong with our distribution system. Some people starve while we cannot get enough for our product to survive. The various papers that were part of the growing together operation that the government put into place made a plea for a structure that would stabilize the food production industry in Canada.
The two plans that are part of this particular bill, the Farm Income Protection Act, are the Gross Revenue Insurance Program and the Net Income Stabilization Account. They are the product of a considerable amount of discussion among people interested in farming and among farmers themselves. At least that was what was supposed to happen. However, the consultation process only went so far. It continued up until the basics had been agreed upon, then the details were left to the bureaucrats and the legislation was left to the bureaucrats.
March 27, 1991

The agreements which really make up the key issues in this whole operation of a safety net are between the federal government and the provincial governments, with only marginal impact from the farm groups.
I know the government says this is the product of a considerable amount of consultation, and I guess we have to agree with that. However, this government has also given the term "consultation" a bad name. Therefore, we are always a little suspicious that what we are getting is an opportunity to say something, but nobody is on the other side listening.
This bill is enabling legislation. It allows the federal Minister of Agriculture to make agreements with the provinces and with the producers relative to the provision of safety nets for the products they produce. The parameters of these agreements are supposed to be established in this legislation and these are supposed to be long-term safety nets.
This was not to be an ad hoc solution to the disasters when they arose, but was supposed to be an ongoing, permanent solution to the ups and downs of the agricultural sector. The need for a permanent stabilization program has long been part of the New Democratic Party's policy, as it was a policy of the CCF, which preceded us.
Various attempts have been made over the years to establish programs which would allow this kind of stabilization as far as agriculture is concerned. We have had the Western Grain Stabilization program, the agricultural stabilization program, Crop Insurance Act, various supply management marketing boards. All of these have been attempts to put in place a safety net program that would be permanent and satisfactory.
These attempts have worked with varying degrees of success, supply management probably being the relative easy winner among the groups. In 1985, the Hon. John Wise, then the Minister of Agriculture, made a commitment on behalf of this government to the country that he would put in place a permanent long-term stabilization program for all sectors of agriculture. I am sure John Wise is breathing easier today because I think he gave up in despair of even expanding the supply management under the ideology that was at that particular time espousing things like free trade and the selling of the country.
As it happened, the hon. John Wise left us and it has taken the government since 1985 until now to come up with some kind of an alternative to the suggestion that was put in place at that time.
